 Today is a great day because The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping has finally hit cinemas! 
 Lionsgate
 The second prequel (and sixth in the series) takes us back to the 50th Hunger Games, diving into the life of Haymitch Abernathy before he became the man we know from the original story. We sat down with director Francis Lawrence and producer Nina Jacobson to talk about dystopian worlds, casting beloved characters, and what goes into making such an iconic franchise. 
 BuzzFeed UK
 From the original Hunger Games to this second prequel now, what has been your biggest lesson immersing yourself in the world of Panem?
Francis Lawrence: Wow, honestly, I just feel like every single thing that I've done, there's like some new challenge or something new. And it sort of doesn't matter how many things you've done, how challenging they've been, the kinds of things you've gone through. There's always going to be something. We've done loads of complicated things, but to go and do the chariot sequence, let's say, in this was like something beyond, I think, a sequence that was more complicated than anything any of us had ever done before with the amount of people and horses and chariots and crashes and crowds. So I just feel like each time, it's something new and just an extreme challenge.
 Lionsgate
 Do you like that each one is challenging? I'm sure some people get into a rhythm with franchises, but that’s not the case for you. 
 Nina Jacobson: What I love about the books is that they’re not repetitive or redundant. Each time she's [Suzanne Collins] writing, she has some particular ideas and thematic intentions that she wants to explore and characters who she feels can express those ideas. And so each one is so distinct from the rest.
 Through the scriptwriting process, Suzanne is very closely integrated with us at every moment. We are on the phone every day, working page by page for hundreds of hours. By the time we are done with multiple drafts, we will have spent.
 Then during production, she steps back. And, you know, she doesn't watch daily. She's not on set. And that distance that she has then allows us, when we have the first cut of the film that we're ready to show people, to then share with her and to get the benefit of her having that little bit more distance than we have.
 But all of the inspiration is from her to begin with, and her instincts and what she can see, because we'll get to a place where we're so in it that it's hard to see it from a distance. And yet her instincts and her connection to the audience and what you want to feel, what you want to have happen, how you want things to land is honestly incredible.
 So, I would say that each time I have deeper and greater respect for the perspective and the wisdom that she brings, not just as the author who makes it all possible, but as our partner in turning it into a movie.
 Jason Mendez / Getty Images for Lionsgate
 Francis, you could say you love a dystopian story – I wanted to know what has always attracted you to creating these dystopian worlds because, outside of The Hunger Games , you have The Long Walk and I Am Legend. What is it about those storylines? 
 Francis: I mean, part of it is the world-building. I really love the visual aspect of making movies. And so when you can build a world, whether that's empty New York or the world of The Long Walk or the worlds of The Hunger Games , I think that's really fun.
 There's almost nothing more satisfying than working with great production designers and figuring out what that's going to look like and kind of imagining those worlds. But I also think that they sort of set the stage to tell really interesting, timely, thematic stories and usually really emotional stories. So if you can have a really emotional story that somehow feels relevant but at the same time has scope and world-building, I mean, that's a perfect combo for me. So I think that's kind of the appeal to me.
 Lionsgate
 With this prequel, I can imagine there might have been a bit more pressure with casting, because there are characters that we already know and love. What was the biggest task when it came to casting Sunrise on the Reaping ? What did you find most difficult? 
 Francis: I think the biggest task, and I think the one that we were probably the most worried about, was Haymitch because typically, these movies have a younger, up-and-coming cast and then there's sort of more older, more veteran kind of actors playing other roles.
 And whoever was gonna play Haymitch had big shoes to fill. And it's not just because Woody [Harrelson] did such an amazing job and is a great actor, but also – this kid is gonna be really put through it in this movie. And so we needed to make sure that he could play all the facets we needed.
 That he needed the youthfulness, the optimism, the mischief, the irreverence; that he could be in love, the emotional toll he was gonna have to go through, then sort of leaning into the more sort of cynical, drunk, sarcastic version, damaged version that we're more familiar with.
 He was gonna have to do a lot. And so that was probably the biggest stress, but we found Joe [Zada] relatively early, and we put him through it, but we knew he would be the one.
 And we shot him; I remember it was on our prep day and it was a very simple scene of him climbing a tree, but I just felt very relieved because I sort of felt like, ‘Okay, we're gonna be able to anchor this movie on this kid’. And I think he just did a phenomenal job.
 But the rest, I didn't feel much stress because we had a wish list of actors, and they luckily all said yes. And so that was kind of amazing. So if a bunch of them had said no and we had to start going down a list, it would have probably been a little more stressful, but they luckily all said yes.
 Nina: It was actually incredibly fun. You can't even believe that you do your dream list, and there were actors on there who were on my bucket list of people I always wished I'd gotten to work with. Jesse [Plemons] was on my bucket list. Ralph [Fiennes] was on my bucket list.
 I'd worked with Glenn [Close] before, so we were thrilled to get her. You had worked with Elle [Fanning], and I hadn't, but when you're starting to get the people who say no to everything, and they're saying yes to this, it was incredible.
 And I think our casting department, they just went all out, and I love that they brought as much exuberance and originality to the choices of the young actors as to who we should focus on in those grown-up roles.
 Mike Coppola / Getty Images
 Everyone saying yes speaks to the legacy the franchise has built, because it's just so amazing, and you should both be incredibly proud of it. But now we're at this point where people don't know if there's going to be another film; we don't know where we're going to continue; who knows where we're at. What would you say has been your proudest achievement while making this franchise that you maybe want to share with the fans? 
 Francis: Proudest achievement? I don't know, I mean, weirdly, I always feel like it's the last one, so I think this movie right now is my proudest achievement. I'm really happy with this movie, really proud of it, really happy with the way it turned out.
 I love all the performances, and I love the cast and love the way it looks, and I'm really proud of what it says, and I think what it makes people think about, so I'd probably say this one.
 Nina: Yeah, I would say I feel very proud to get to work on something which has the kind of complexity that these stories do that challenge you, and hopefully people leave the theatre having a conversation and not just sort of being lulled by spectacle, but engaged and provoked, and they're subversive.
 And so to pull that off, I would also say this collaboration and the fact that we have had this long run together, Frances, Suzanne, and I, with this crew that we've managed to really make a family out of it that keeps coming together.
 It's very rare, honestly. Sequels, oftentimes, everyone is way bigger than the last one, and there's a whole bunch of new people, and so just this little unit that has come together and that keeps coming together where people just come and give everything they've got and with such open hearts. These movies are built from that little family.
 Francis: Because it's a franchise, I think a lot of times people come into it and think that, like other franchises, it may be sort of built by some sort of corporate structure. And I think a lot of actors, and especially ones who maybe aren't so familiar, come in and realise, like, oh no, it's really just me and Nina on set. And then a crew that's very familiar with each other, but there’s not a bunch of suits looking over our shoulders and making decisions by committee. It really is made by a family.
 The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping is in cinemas now!
